description: Learning cards with subtitle, body paragraphs, and takeaway per card.

cards.title: Four Elements Explain All Good Cooking
cards.subtitle: You follow the recipe perfectly. It still tastes wrong because you didn't understand what the recipe was actually doing.
body: Every dish that's ever tasted good used some combination of salt, fat, acid, and heat. Not as ingredients—as tools.
The recipe told you what to add. It didn't tell you why those things work.
cards.takeaway: Every cuisine on earth uses the same four levers.

cards.title: Salt Is Not Just Seasoning
cards.subtitle: The tomato tastes like nothing. You add salt. Now it tastes like tomato.
body: Undersalted food doesn't taste less salty. It tastes flat and muted. Salt doesn't add flavor—it unlocks what's already there.

• The tomato had the flavor
• You just couldn't taste it
• The most common home cooking mistake is undersalting
cards.takeaway: Food that tastes 'missing something' usually needs salt.

cards.title: Fat Carries Flavor
cards.subtitle: You toast the spices in a dry pan. They smell good for ten seconds, then fade.
body: Flavor compounds dissolve in fat, not water. Toast spices in oil and the flavor stays. Toast them dry and it vanishes.
Fat isn't just richness—it's the vehicle that carries flavor to your tongue.
cards.takeaway: The same ingredients in water taste muted.

cards.title: Acid Balances Everything
cards.subtitle: The stew is rich and well-seasoned. It still tastes heavy. You squeeze lemon over it and everything sharpens.
body: Fat and salt make food taste full. Acid makes it taste awake. The stew had everything it needed except contrast.
Heavy dishes need brightness. Flat dishes need sharpness.
cards.takeaway: Acid cuts through richness and creates contrast.

cards.title: Heat Is the Final Variable
cards.subtitle: Same chicken. High heat makes it crispy and dry. Low heat makes it tender and bland. You wanted both.
body: The temperature you choose decides the texture you get. High heat browns and crisps. Low heat tenderizes and melts.

• You can't have both at once unless you use both at different times
• High heat builds crust, low heat builds tenderness
cards.takeaway: Temperature is a choice with consequences.

cards.title: Season From Within, Not After
cards.subtitle: You salt the steak after it's cooked. The outside is salty. The inside tastes like nothing.
body: Salt needs time to move inward. Surface salt stays surface salt unless you give it time to dissolve and migrate.
Salting pasta water seasons the noodle itself. Salting after cooking seasons your tongue.
cards.takeaway: Timing changes where the salt goes.

cards.title: Tasting Is the Only Reliable Measurement
cards.subtitle: The recipe says one teaspoon. Your tomatoes are more acidic than hers were. You follow the recipe anyway.
body: Recipes assume average ingredients. Your ingredients aren't average. Her salt crystals were larger. Your tomatoes are sharper.
The numbers can't account for that. Your tongue can.
cards.takeaway: Tasting is the only way to adjust for reality.

cards.title: Fat Decides Texture
cards.subtitle: You use melted butter in the pie crust because it's easier. The crust is dense, not flaky.
body: Cold butter creates flaky layers. Melted butter creates tenderness. The fat was the same. The temperature changed the structure.

• Texture isn't about the ingredient
• It's about how you handle it
• Cold fat makes layers, melted fat makes smooth
cards.takeaway: The method decides the outcome.

cards.title: Crispy Means the Water Left
cards.subtitle: The chicken skin stays pale and rubbery. You didn't dry it first.
body: Crispiness is what happens when surface water evaporates. Wet skin can't crisp—it has to boil off the moisture first.
By the time the water leaves, the cooking window passed. Pat it dry before it goes in.
cards.takeaway: Crispy is what's left when water isn't.

cards.title: Browning Is Flavor Being Built
cards.subtitle: The vegetables are soft but pale. They cooked, but they didn't brown. They taste flat.
body: Browning creates new flavors that don't exist in the raw ingredient. Pale food is cooked but not interesting.
The heat was too low or the pan was too crowded. Color equals flavor.
cards.takeaway: If it doesn't brown, it won't taste right.

cards.title: Acid Wakes Up Flat Food
cards.subtitle: The dish tastes okay but forgettable. You add a squeeze of lime and suddenly it's alive.
body: Rich food without acid feels one-note. The flavor is there but it sits heavy. Acid cuts through and creates contrast.

• The difference is immediate and obvious
• Heavy needs bright
• When food tastes boring, acid is usually the missing piece
cards.takeaway: A squeeze of citrus can transform a dish.

cards.title: Salt Early, Salt Often
cards.subtitle: You salt the finished dish. Every bite tastes salty at first, then bland.
body: Salt added at the end sits on the surface. Salt added throughout moves inward.
The same total amount distributed across cooking stages tastes balanced. All at once tastes harsh then empty.
cards.takeaway: Seasoned food and salty food are not the same.

cards.title: Residual Heat Keeps Cooking
cards.subtitle: The steak hits 135°F. You pull it off. By the time you cut into it, it's 142°F and overcooked.
body: Heat doesn't stop when the flame turns off. The outside is hotter than the inside, and that heat keeps moving inward.
Dense food holds more heat. Small food cools faster. Carryover cooking is predictable.
cards.takeaway: Pull it early or it arrives late.

cards.title: Dry Ingredients Brown, Wet Ingredients Steam
cards.subtitle: Water boils at 212°F. Browning starts at 280°F. The wet steak never gets there.
body: Surface moisture has to boil off before browning can start. The pan hisses and steams—that's water leaving, not flavor forming.

• Only when the surface dries does the temperature climb high enough to brown
• Wet food steams first
cards.takeaway: Dry the surface or skip the sear.

cards.title: Emulsions Are Fragile Agreements
cards.subtitle: The vinaigrette looks smooth when you shake it. Thirty seconds later it's separated into oil and vinegar again.
body: Fat and water don't want to stay mixed. An emulsifier forces them together temporarily. But the agreement is fragile.
Wrong temperature, wrong ratio, wrong speed and it breaks. Egg yolk, mustard, and lecithin broker the truce.
cards.takeaway: Emulsions require maintenance or they quit.

cards.title: Your Palate Is Trainable
cards.subtitle: You taste the sauce and can't tell what's wrong. She tastes it and says 'needs acid.' You add lemon. She's right.
body: Tasting well isn't a gift. It's practice. She's tasted more sauces, made more adjustments, built a vocabulary for what balance feels like.
Taste before and after every change. Notice what shifts.
cards.takeaway: Tasting is a skill that improves with repetition.

cards.title: Recipes Are Maps, Not Laws
cards.subtitle: The recipe says high heat. Your stove runs hot. You follow it anyway and burn the garlic.
body: Recipes assume average equipment and average ingredients. You don't have either. The recipe shows one path.

• You need to understand why that path works
• So you can adjust when your conditions differ
• Your kitchen isn't their kitchen
cards.takeaway: Understanding the why lets you adapt the how.

cards.title: Mise en Place Is Thinking Before Doing
cards.subtitle: The garlic burns while you're still chopping the onions. Everything happens faster than you expected.
body: Cooking moves fast. If you're prepping while the pan is hot, you're always behind.
Chop everything first. Measure everything first. Then turn on the heat and work calmly.
cards.takeaway: Burnt garlic happens when you confuse the two.

cards.title: Tough Cuts Need Time, Tender Cuts Need Speed
cards.subtitle: You braise the expensive steak for three hours. It's dry and stringy. The cheap cut would have worked.
body: Tough cuts have collagen that melts into gelatin with time. Tender cuts have no collagen—just lean muscle that dries out.
The method that saves one ruins the other. Collagen needs hours at low heat. Lean meat needs minutes at high heat.
cards.takeaway: Match the method to the cut, not the price.

cards.title: Balance Is the Whole Point
cards.subtitle: The dish has enough salt, enough fat, enough acid. It still doesn't work. Nothing is in balance.
body: Each element present doesn't mean each element in proportion. Too much salt makes it harsh. Too much fat makes it heavy.

• The right amount of each, in relation to the others, makes it whole
• Balance isn't equal amounts—it's right proportions
cards.takeaway: Every adjustment changes what the others need to be.
